1.pericope_label: Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel came
debates: What being at ease is blamed for
Who exactly is addressed
What the title chief of the nations means
outliers: Clarke would change one letter so that the word means leaning confidently rather than dwelling at ease
Calvin explains the indifference of the great by the profit they take from public calamity, since war and famine enrich the men who deal in them
themes: A woe pronounced on what the world calls happiness
Church privileges used as a mattress
A hill that grew as holy as the holy hill
Men who grow fat while the poor are burdened

2.pericope_label: Pass ye unto Calneh, and see; and from thence go ye to Hamath the great: then go down to Gath of the Philistines: be they better than these kingdoms? or their border greater than your border? Ye that put far away the evil day, and cause the seat of violence to come near
debates: Whether the three cities are named as ruins or as rivals
Which way the comparison of borders runs
What putting far away the evil day amounts to
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch deny that the verse can refer to cities already destroyed, against the reading the other voices assume
Calvin illustrates the folly with a drunkard who laughs at the physician warning him of the fever he is drinking towards
themes: Ruined capitals held up as a mirror
A border no larger than the one that will be lost
A day of reckoning always thought distant
Judges strengthening themselves in their own tyranny

4.pericope_label: That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall; That chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David
debates: Whether luxury as such is what is condemned
What the chanting was
Whether the comparison with David praises or blames him
outliers: Clarke reads the verse as a reproof of David himself for bringing so many instruments into worship, where Calvin denies that music is condemned at all
Calvin dates the arrival of ivory beds in Italy to a particular conquest, to show that the same furniture may be costly in one country and common in another
themes: Beds inlaid with what a court can afford
Furniture that is innocent until the country is starving
A voice quivering to match twelve strings
New instruments invented for an old amusement

6.pericope_label: That drink wine in bowls, and anoint themselves with the chief ointments: but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph. Therefore now shall they go captive with the first that go captive, and the banquet of them that stretched themselves shall be removed
debates: What is reprehended in the drinking bowls
Why anointing is blamed when it is not sinful
Who goes first into captivity and why
outliers: Clarke suggests the cost of the vessels rather than the quantity drunk is the fault reproved
Ellicott notes that the word for these bowls is the one used elsewhere of the basons of sacrifice
themes: Bowls used where cups would do
An ointment innocent in any other year
Men who feel nothing for a ruined country
The head of the procession into exile

8.pericope_label: The Lord God hath sworn by himself, saith the Lord the God of hosts, I abhor the excellency of Jacob, and hate his palaces: therefore will I deliver up the city with all that is therein
debates: Why the oath is sworn by himself
What the excellency of Jacob is
Whether the word for it is used in a good or a bad sense
outliers: Ellicott narrows the excellency to the shrine at Samaria with its offerings and calf-worship
Calvin insists the word is used in a good sense, so that the point is the worthlessness of privilege rather than the sin of pride
themes: An oath with nothing greater to swear by
Privileges that become abominable when trusted
A dignity stripped off and counted as nothing
A city handed over with everything in it

9.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, if there remain ten men in one house, that they shall die. And a man’s uncle shall take him up, and he that burneth him, to bring out the bones out of the house, and shall say unto him that is by the sides of the house, Is there yet any with thee? and he shall say, No. Then shall he say, Hold thy tongue: for we may not make mention of the name of the Lord
debates: What the number ten signifies
Why a kinsman does the burying
Why the survivor is told to be silent
outliers: Calvin reconstructs the scene so that the uncle burns the bodies indoors in order to carry out only the bones
Clarke reports an authority who reads the whole verse as the effects of famine and pestilence during a siege
themes: A household of ten with nobody left to mourn
A servile office falling to the heir
Bones carried out because a body is too heavy
A name that may not be spoken aloud

11.pericope_label: For, behold, the Lord commandeth, and he will smite the great house with breaches, and the little house with clefts. Shall horses run upon the rock? will one plow there with oxen? for ye have turned judgment into gall, and the fruit of righteousness into hemlock
debates: What the two sizes of house mark
Why horses and rocks are the figure chosen
What the two bitter plants are
outliers: Clarke gives four separate reasons why the image is absurd, beginning with the fact that horses were then unshod
Ellicott corrects hemlock to wormwood, on the ground that the same word is so rendered everywhere else
themes: Death knocking at cottage and tower alike
Walls that crack because the earth will not hold
A horse race over bare rock
Justice turned into a bitter weed

13.pericope_label: Ye which rejoice in a thing of nought, which say, Have we not taken to us horns by our own strength? But, behold, I will raise up against you a nation, O house of Israel, saith the Lord the God of hosts; and they shall afflict you from the entering in of Hemath unto the river of the wilderness
debates: What the thing of nought is
What the horns stand for
How far the threatened invasion reaches
outliers: Gill includes works of righteousness among the things of nought, with a careful distinction about when they are not
Ellicott observes that the region marked out for invasion is exactly the region a recent king had won, so that the conquest is measured by the boast
themes: Riches counted as things that are not
Wine that furnishes the poor with horns
A frontier named by the victory that reached it
A spacious country made strait everywhere
